property_summary: Calling SetMinSum with any value sets MinSum equal to that value (i.e., MinSum == arg) when contract is not initialized.
When the contract is uninitialized, calling SetMinSum(x) sets MinSum equal to x (it does not depend on prior MinSum).
When contract is not initialized, a single call to SetMinSum(x) results in MinSum being at least x (i.e., MinSum >= x).
If the contract is not yet initialized, a single call to SetMinSum(x) makes MinSum equal to x (i.e., MinSum does not depend on prior MinSum).

Invariant: calling Collect(...) does not change MinSum (reference sets MinSum exactly once via SetMinSum and Collect never mutates it); the mutant that adds to MinSum in SetMinSum can lead to a different MinSum observed after Collect for some fuzzed inputs because repeated or unexpected initialization interactions change MinSum in the mutant but not the reference.
SetMinSum can be successfully called (does not revert) before Initialized() is called, so calling SetMinSum prior to Initialized must succeed.

Invariant: once Initialized() has not been called, calling SetMinSum must succeed exactly once in the reference (subsequent calls revert due to the 'intitalized' guard), while the mutant allows repeated successful calls that change MinSum; thus for some fuzzed _val the mutant's MinSum after two calls will differ from the reference which still reverts on the second call.

For any uint _val, calling SetMinSum twice: the reference C reverts on the second call (so the second call does not succeed), whereas the mutant allows the second call to succeed and update MinSum; therefore the reference guarantees the second SetMinSum call fails, which the mutant breaks for some _val.

For any caller and any value, calling SetMinSum when intitalized == false always succeeds and leaves MinSum equal to the supplied _val; the mutant that writes MinSum before checking intitalized can revert after writing and thus for some inputs (when intitalized == true) would have attempted to set MinSum but must revert, causing a difference in observable MinSum/state.

For any caller and any value, calling SetMinSum on an uninitialized contract either (a) succeeds and leaves MinSum equal to the supplied value, or (b) if the contract is already initialized, the call MUST revert and must NOT leave MinSum changed; the mutant that sets MinSum before reverting can cause MinSum to observeably differ after a call that reverts, violating that invariant.

For all inputs, calling SetMinSum succeeds iff the contract is not initialized, and when it succeeds MinSum equals the provided value; the mutant that assigns MinSum before reverting can cause a reverted call when initialized but would have set MinSum (if reversion didn't undo), so the observable behavior (success vs revert and stored MinSum after attempts) differs for some input where intitalized==true.

For every caller and value, calling SetMinSum on an initialized contract MUST revert and MUST NOT change MinSum; the mutant that writes MinSum before reverting can leave MinSum different after the call (i.e., the reference guarantees that any call that returns/throws when initialized does not change MinSum, but the mutant violates this for calls made when initialized).

For any caller and value, calling SetMinSum either (A) succeeds and leaves MinSum equal to the supplied value when the contract is not initialized, or (B) if the contract is initialized the call must revert and must NOT succeed — i.e. the boolean success of SetMinSum equals (not initialized); the mutant makes SetMinSum revert when initialized but a naive observation of the call success boolean distinguishes behavior because the reference will always return false (revert) when initialized and true otherwise, while the mutant will also revert when initialized but still the success boolean observed via try/catch remains reliable — thus we assert that a call's success flag equals (!initialized) after invoking Initialized() or not, and the mutant is found because it changes the observed MinSum after a reverted call (we detect this by checking success flag and MinSum consistency).

After calling SetLogFile(x) before initialization, the contract's LogFile getter returns the same address that was passed in; the mutant that casts to address(0) breaks this by always setting LogFile to address(0) for some inputs.

For any non-zero address A passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract stores LogFile as A (getter returns A) while the mutant that always casts to address(0) will make the getter return address(0) for some such A, so the stored LogFile equals the provided address is the invariant the reference satisfies and the mutant breaks.

For any address A passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract stores LogFile as that same address (the getter returns A); the mutant that casts to address(0) breaks this because it will set LogFile to address(0) instead of A for some inputs.

For any caller address X and provided Log contract address L (which may be a contract), after calling SetLogFile(L) on the correct contract (before initialization) the stored LogFile getter must be a contract address whose codehash equals the codehash of L; the mutant that writes address(0) breaks this when L is a real contract (non-empty code).

For every non-zero addr L passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference stores a LogFile whose address is non-zero (has some non-zero address getter), whereas the mutant that always assigns Log(address(0)) can make the stored LogFile address equal to zero for some L — so the invariant is: after SetLogFile(L) with L != address(0), address of c.LogFile() != address(0).

For any caller address X passed to SetLogFile, the reference sets LogFile to the provided _log address; the mutant instead sets LogFile to msg.sender, so there exist inputs where LogFile != _log (i.e., when caller != _log) and thus the mutant violates the rule.

For any caller and provided address, the correct contract stores LogFile equal to the provided address passed to SetLogFile; the mutant stores msg.sender instead, so when caller != provided address the mutant differs.

For every call to SetLogFile(_log) the reference contract records LogFile == _log; the mutant records LogFile == msg.sender, so when the caller is different from the provided _log address the mutant will differ.

For every call to SetLogFile(_log) the reference contract stores LogFile equal to the provided _log address; the mutant stores msg.sender instead, so when the caller is different from the provided _log address the mutant will differ.

For every call to SetLogFile(_log) the correct contract stores LogFile == _log (the provided address); the mutant stores msg.sender instead, so when the caller != _log the mutant will make LogFile != _log.
For any address passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the contract's LogFile getter is updated to that address; the mutant that removes the assignment leaves LogFile unchanged for some inputs.

For any address arg passed to SetLogFile before Initialized() is called, the contract's public LogFile getter updates to that address; the mutant that removes the assignment leaves LogFile unchanged for some address inputs.

For any address A passed to SetLogFile before Initialized() is called, the reference contract updates its LogFile getter to A (so address(c.LogFile()) == A) but the mutant that removed the assignment will leave LogFile unchanged for some inputs, so this property will fail for those inputs.

For any address X passed to SetLogFile while the contract is uninitialized, the reference stores X as LogFile (address(c.LogFile())==X) but the mutant that removed the assignment will sometimes leave LogFile unchanged, so asserting that SetLogFile returns the provided address distinguishes them.

Before Initialized() is called, calling SetLogFile with any nonzero address must make address(c.LogFile()) equal that address (the reference assigns LogFile while the mutant does not, so for some addresses the getter will differ).

For any address input, calling SetLogFile stores the exact address value in the contract's LogFile slot such that the public getter for Acc (unmodified) still reveals the same address when encoded via the Log type; the mutant that re-casts via address(uint160(_log)) can change the stored address value for addresses outside 160-bit range casting differences and thus breaks equality for some inputs — the test checks that after SetLogFile the address retrieved via the stored LogFile equals the input address (by reading the stored address through the LogFile public getter behaviour), which holds for the reference but fails for the mutant for some fuzzed addresses.

For any provided address _log, after calling SetLogFile(_log) the stored LogFile address (read back by assigning it to an address via the public getter pattern) equals the original _log; the mutant re-casts via address(uint160(_log)) can change the stored value for some inputs and thus violates this equality.

For any provided address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract stores a LogFile pointer whose address, when read back via converting the contract's public LogFile getter result to address, exactly equals the original _log; the mutant that casts via address(uint160(_log)) can truncate non-canonical 256-bit addresses and thus will differ for some fuzzed addresses.

For any provided address _log, after calling SetLogFile(_log) the stored LogFile pointer (read back via the public getter that returns the Log contract) converts to the same address as the original _log; the mutant that casts via address(uint160(_log)) can change/truncate the stored address for some fuzzed addresses and thus breaks this equality.

For any provided address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract stores a LogFile reference whose address converted via address(c.LogFile()) equals the original _log; the mutant that re-casts using address(uint160(_log)) can change that stored address for some 256-bit addresses and thus violates this equality for some inputs.

For any address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract sets LogFile to _log (including address(0)); the mutant leaves LogFile unchanged when _log == address(0), so there exist inputs (passing address(0)) where the mutant's LogFile differs.

For every input address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract sets the public LogFile to _log (including address(0)); the mutant fails to set LogFile when _log == address(0), leaving the prior value unchanged.

For any address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on a fresh (uninitialized) contract sets the public LogFile getter to exactly _log (including address(0)); the mutant leaves LogFile unchanged when called with address(0), violating this rule for that input.

For any address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on a fresh, un-initialized C sets the public LogFile getter to _log; the mutant leaves LogFile unchanged when _log == address(0), so there exists an input (address(0)) where the mutant violates this rule.

For any address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on a fresh, uninitialized contract sets the public LogFile getter to exactly _log; the mutant leaves LogFile unchanged when given address(0), so there exist inputs (notably address(0)) that make the mutant disagree.

After any Put by an address, the holder's unlockTime is set to the maximum of its previous unlockTime and (block.timestamp + _lockTime); the mutant inverts the comparison so it may set unlockTime to a smaller value when _lockTime would produce a later unlock, breaking this monotonic non-decreasing rule.
